annotation: The model treated the widowed head as a qualifying surviving spouse even though no dependent child is listed. That gave it the $32,000/$44,000 joint Social Security thresholds (taxable SS of $11,542 instead of $18,542.70) and a $32,300 joint standard deduction plus a $1,650 aged add-on. Single status gives $18,150 plus the $6,000 senior deduction against AGI of $50,437.11, so taxable income is $26,287.11 and tax is $2,906.45, reaching into the 12% bracket.

The model computed taxable SS ($18,542) and AGI ($50,436) correctly. It then used surviving-spouse joint status without a dependent child and took the $32,200 joint standard deduction plus the $1,650 aged add-on. A single filer's deductions are $16,100 + $2,050 + $6,000 senior = $24,150, leaving $26,287.11 taxable and $2,906.45 of tax, not $10,586 taxed entirely at 10%.

The model put the nontaxable $48,000 of veterans benefits into gross income, taxed Social Security at the 85% cap, and subtracted ESI premiums even though there are no wages. It then dropped its own estimate of about $6,600 and asserted zero tax without any computation. The correct figures are AGI of $50,437.11, $24,150 of single standard, aged and senior deductions, $26,287.11 of taxable income and $2,906.45 of tax.

The model filed single and applied the correct $18,150 standard deduction and $6,000 senior deduction, but it misapplied the Social Security worksheet. It added half of benefits ($13,048) to 85% of the excess over $34,000, where the worksheet adds the lesser of $4,500 and half of benefits, so it taxed the full $22,182 cap instead of $18,542.70. It also ended the 10% bracket at $12,150 instead of the 2026 threshold of $12,400, which produced $29,926 of taxable income and $3,348 of tax.

The model assumed qualifying-surviving-spouse (joint) status without a dependent child and taxed Social Security at the 85% cap. It then declared taxable income near zero, although its own figures ($54,076 AGI minus about $40,000 of deductions) leave roughly $14,000 taxable. As a single filer, the head's AGI of $50,437.11 less $24,150 of deductions leaves $26,287.11 taxable and $2,906.45 of tax.

The model filed single and totaled the correct $24,150 of standard, aged and senior deductions. It taxed Social Security at the 85% cap ($22,182) instead of $18,542.70, which is $4,500 plus 85% of the excess over $34,000. It then dropped its own bracket result of about $3,300 and asserted $1,176, claiming the senior and standard deductions reduce the tax further even though both were already subtracted; correct taxable income of $26,287.11 yields $2,906.45.

The model computed taxable SS ($18,542) and AGI ($50,436) correctly but filed as a surviving spouse with no dependent child. It therefore applied joint brackets and the $32,200 joint standard deduction plus the $1,650 aged add-on. As a single filer the deductions are $18,150 + $6,000 = $24,150, leaving $26,287.11 taxable into the 12% bracket for $2,906.45.

The model treated the head as a qualifying surviving spouse without a dependent child and used MFJ Social Security thresholds with an estimated $31,550 joint standard deduction. It also taxed the full 85% cap ($22,182), even though its own $44,000-threshold formula gives $11,542, and it omitted the $6,000 OBBBA senior deduction. Single status yields AGI of $50,437.11, $24,150 of deductions and $2,906.45 of tax.

The model filed as a qualifying surviving spouse with a $33,850 joint standard deduction despite having no dependent child. It taxed Social Security at the 85% cap without applying the tier formula and omitted the $6,000 senior deduction. It then raised its own 10%-bracket result of $2,023 to $3,204 with no supporting arithmetic, while single status gives $26,287.11 of taxable income and $2,906.45 of tax.

The model got taxable SS ($18,542) and AGI right but assumed surviving-spouse status with no dependent child. It therefore took the $32,200 joint standard deduction plus the $1,650 aged amount and taxed everything at 10%. Single filing gives $16,100 + $2,050 + $6,000 = $24,150 of deductions, $26,287.11 taxable, and $2,906.45 through the 12% bracket.

The model filed single and computed taxable SS and AGI correctly, but it used a $15,400 base standard deduction; the 2026 single amount is $16,100, or $18,150 with the $2,050 aged add-on. It also omitted the $6,000 OBBBA senior deduction for filers 65 and older. Together these left $32,986 taxable instead of $26,287.11, and it additionally ended the 10% bracket at $12,025 rather than $12,400.

The model taxed Social Security at the 85% cap ($22,182) instead of $4,500 plus 85% of the $16,520 excess over $34,000 ($18,542.70). It also used a $17,350 standard deduction instead of $18,150 and omitted the $6,000 senior deduction, giving $36,726 of taxable income versus $26,287.11. Its bracket step also used a $12,200 top for the 10% bracket instead of $12,400.

The model assumed the TCJA expired in 2026, so it applied a $5,300 personal exemption and a 15% second bracket. OBBBA made the TCJA structure permanent: there is no personal exemption, the second bracket is 12%, and a single 77-year-old gets the $18,150 standard deduction plus the $6,000 senior deduction. The model also itemized the $8,389 ESI premiums as a medical expense, but the itemized total is only $17,587.20 of property and sales taxes, which falls below the standard deduction.

The model filed single with the correct AGI and the correct $18,150 age-65+ standard deduction but never applied the $6,000 OBBBA senior deduction. That left taxable income at $32,286 instead of $26,287.11. It also ended the 10% bracket at $12,200 rather than the 2026 threshold of $12,400.

The model assumed the TCJA expired in 2026 and applied a $5,300 personal exemption and a 15% bracket. It itemized $16,470 of real estate taxes plus $4,606 of ESI premiums as medical expenses. Under OBBBA's permanent TCJA rules there is no personal exemption and the second bracket is 12%, and the $18,150 standard deduction plus the $6,000 senior deduction exceeds the $17,587.20 of itemized property and sales taxes, leaving $26,287.11 taxable and $2,906.45 of tax.

The model's taxable income of $37,990 equals $54,076 of AGI (Social Security taxed at the 85% cap) less only about $16,100, which drops the $2,050 aged add-on and the $6,000 senior deduction. Its $1,109 tax does not follow from its own taxable income either, because the single 10%/12% brackets would give about $4,311. The correct figures are $26,287.11 of taxable income and $2,906.45 of tax.

The model computed AGI correctly but assumed pre-TCJA law returned in 2026, so it itemized $16,470 of real estate taxes, added a $5,400 personal exemption and used a 15% bracket. OBBBA kept the TCJA structure, which has no personal exemption and a 12% bracket. The $18,150 age-adjusted standard deduction plus the $6,000 senior deduction apply, giving $26,287.11 of taxable income and $2,906.45 of tax.

The model assumed the TCJA reverted in 2026, so it itemized $16,470 of real estate taxes, took a $5,050 personal exemption, and used a 15% rate above $11,000. Under OBBBA's permanent rules there is no personal exemption, the brackets are 10% up to $12,400 and 12% above, and the $18,150 standard deduction plus the $6,000 senior deduction beats itemizing. That leaves $26,287.11 taxable and $2,906.45 of tax.

The model asserted that income falls below the standard deduction without computing taxable Social Security or AGI. AGI is $50,437.11, including $18,542.70 of taxable SS, and it exceeds the $24,150 of single standard, aged and senior deductions by $26,287.11, which produces $2,906.45 of tax.

The model computed AGI correctly but applied pre-TCJA rules, itemizing $16,470 of real estate taxes and subtracting a personal exemption to reach $28,666 of taxable income. OBBBA made the TCJA framework permanent, which removes the personal exemption. The single filer takes the $18,150 standard deduction plus the $6,000 senior deduction, giving $26,287.11 taxable and $2,906.45 at 10%/12%.

The model assumed TCJA expiration: it itemized $16,470 of real estate taxes, took a personal exemption and applied 10% and 15% brackets. Under current law there is no personal exemption and the brackets are 10% up to $12,400 and 12% above. The $18,150 standard deduction plus the $6,000 senior deduction applies instead of itemizing, leaving $26,287.11 taxable and $2,906.45 of tax.

The model filed single with the correct AGI but used a $17,000 age-65+ standard deduction instead of $18,150 ($16,100 + $2,050). It also omitted the $6,000 OBBBA senior deduction, leaving $33,436 taxable instead of $26,287.11.

The model filed single with the correct AGI, but it estimated a $17,510 standard deduction instead of the 2026 amount of $16,100 + $2,050 = $18,150, and it omitted the $6,000 OBBBA senior deduction. It also ended the 10% bracket at $12,283 instead of $12,400. Its taxable income came to $32,926 instead of $26,287.11.

The model filed single with the correct AGI and 2026 brackets. It itemized $21,076 by counting the $8,389 ESI premiums as a deductible medical expense and never applied the $6,000 OBBBA senior deduction. Without the premiums, itemized deductions of $17,587.20 (property and sales taxes) fall below the $18,150 standard deduction, and the senior deduction brings total deductions to $24,150 and taxable income to $26,287.11.

The model asserted, without computing anything, that the age-65 standard deduction and a surviving-spouse rate structure offset all income. The head files single, so AGI of $50,437.11 less $24,150 of standard, aged and senior deductions leaves $26,287.11 taxable, producing $2,906.45.

The model claimed the standard deduction for a 77-year-old offsets all income without computing taxable Social Security or AGI. AGI is $50,437.11, and the $18,150 standard deduction plus the $6,000 senior deduction leave $26,287.11 taxable, which gives $2,906.45 of tax.

The model applied surviving-spouse (joint) thresholds even though no dependent child is listed. That cut taxable SS to $11,542 instead of $18,542.70, and it took the $32,200 joint standard deduction plus the $1,650 aged add-on and the senior deduction. As a single filer, AGI is $50,437.11, deductions are $24,150, and $26,287.11 of taxable income yields $2,906.45.

The model computed taxable Social Security as about $18,592 instead of $18,542.70 ($4,500 plus 85% of the provisional income excess over $34,000). That inflated AGI to $50,486 and taxable income to $26,336 against the correct $26,287.11. The extra $49 taxed at 12% gives $2,912.34 instead of $2,906.45.

The model used surviving-spouse filing status without a qualifying dependent child. Its $359 matches about $3,590 of taxable income at 10%, which is what joint Social Security thresholds and the joint standard deduction plus the aged add-on and senior deduction produce. Single status leaves $26,287.11 taxable and $2,906.45 of tax.

The model computed taxable SS ($18,542) and AGI correctly but used surviving-spouse status with no dependent child, taking a $33,850 joint age-adjusted standard deduction. The single deduction is $18,150, so with the $6,000 senior deduction taxable income is $26,287.11 rather than $10,586, and the tax is $2,906.45.

The model used the correct single structure and deductions but reached $26,336 of taxable income instead of $26,287.11. That comes from overstating taxable Social Security by about $49 relative to $18,542.70 ($4,500 plus 85% of provisional income above $34,000). The extra income at 12% pushes the tax to $2,912 instead of $2,906.45.

The model claimed senior deductions and credits exceed taxable income without computing either. AGI of $50,437.11 less the $18,150 standard deduction and the $6,000 senior deduction leaves $26,287.11 taxable. No nonrefundable credit offsets the resulting $2,906.45, because the elderly credit is eliminated by the nontaxable Social Security and the AGI.

The model assumed post-TCJA-sunset law, adding a $5,300 personal exemption to a $16,600 + $1,600 standard deduction and applying a 15% rate. It used the joint 10% bracket top of $23,200 as a qualifying surviving spouse despite having no dependent child, and it omitted the $6,000 senior deduction. Under OBBBA law the single filer deducts $18,150 + $6,000, and $26,287.11 is taxed at 10% up to $12,400 and 12% above.

The model computed AGI correctly but assumed the pre-TCJA regime returned in 2026, itemizing $16,470 of property tax, taking a personal exemption, and using 10% and 15% brackets. OBBBA made the TCJA rules permanent, so the single filer takes the $18,150 standard deduction plus the $6,000 senior deduction with no exemption. That leaves $26,287.11 taxed at 10%/12% for $2,906.45.

The model reached the correct $26,286 of taxable income through single status, the $18,150 standard deduction and the $6,000 senior deduction. It then ended the 10% bracket at $12,200 instead of the 2026 single threshold of $12,400, which moved $200 from the 10% rate to the 12% rate. The result was $2,910.32, rounded to $2,910, instead of $1,240 + 12% × $13,887.11 = $2,906.45.

The model assumed the TCJA sunset in 2026, so it dropped the SALT cap, itemized $16,470 of property taxes plus $4,606 of ESI premiums as medical, and applied a 15% bracket. Under OBBBA's permanent rules the brackets are 10% and 12%, and the itemized total is $17,587.20 of property and sales taxes. That falls below the $18,150 standard deduction, which together with the $6,000 senior deduction gives $26,287.11 taxable and $2,906.45 of tax.
The model returned no value and no explanation for federal_income_tax_before_refundable_credits, so there was no answer to score against the $2,906.45 reference.

The model started from gross income that included the full $26,096 of Social Security, subtracted a rough standard deduction, and then netted out a $750 elderly credit and an inapplicable lifetime learning credit to reach zero. The Credit for the Elderly is zero here because the nontaxable Social Security exceeds the initial amount. The taxable income of $26,287.11 (AGI $50,437.11 less $24,150) carries $2,906.45 of tax with no nonrefundable credit to offset it.

The model left half of Social Security out of provisional income, which it put at $37,472 instead of $50,520, and dropped the $4,500 tier-one amount, so it taxed only $2,951.20 of benefits instead of $18,542.70. Its single filing status and $24,150 of deductions were correct, but the understated AGI of $34,845.20 left only $10,695.20 taxable instead of $26,287.11.

The model treated all Social Security as nontaxable on the claim that provisional income stays below the base amount, when provisional income is $50,520 and $18,542.70 of benefits is taxable. It also used a $31,150 qualifying-widow(er) deduction despite having no dependent child and omitted the $6,000 senior deduction. The correct figures are AGI of $50,437.11, $24,150 of deductions and $2,906.45 of tax.

The model claimed the single 65+ standard deduction eliminates taxable income without computing taxable Social Security or AGI. The $18,150 standard deduction plus the $6,000 senior deduction against $50,437.11 of AGI leaves $26,287.11 taxable, which yields $2,906.45.
All wrong responses were missing or unparseable predictions.

The model treated age 77 and an asserted income exclusion calculation as sufficient for Texas aged Medicaid without identifying or satisfying an aged eligibility pathway. The person qualifies through no Medicaid category and receives no SSI, so the claimed below-threshold aged eligibility does not apply.

The model correctly stated that no earned wages were reported and that payroll tax therefore equals zero, but then submitted $1,534 instead. Its numeric output contradicts its own payroll-tax-base analysis and the required final-value contract.
The model returned no payroll_tax value or explanation, so the required output was missing.

It computed AGI of $31,402.25 correctly but assumed the TCJA had sunset. So it used a $16,600 joint standard deduction plus $3,300 in aged additions, and added $10,600 in personal exemptions. That left $902.25 of taxable income. Under the permanent TCJA structure from P.L. 119-21, exemptions are $0 and the 2026 joint standard deduction is $32,200, which by itself exceeds AGI, so taxable income and tax are $0.

It explicitly assumed the TCJA sunset in 2026. It deducted a projected $15,150 standard deduction, $3,100 in aged additions and $10,100 in personal exemptions, totaling $28,350, which left $3,052.25 taxed at 10%. P.L. 119-21 kept personal exemptions at $0 and set the 2026 joint standard deduction at $32,200, which is above the $31,402.25 AGI, so tax is $0.

It applied pre-TCJA-style deductions for 2026: a $19,600 standard deduction including the aged additions, plus $10,000 in personal exemptions. That left $1,802.25 of taxable income. Personal exemptions remain $0 permanently under P.L. 119-21, and the 2026 joint standard deduction of $32,200 alone wipes out the $31,402.25 AGI, before the aged addition and the $6,000-per-senior deduction.

It reasoned 'after TCJA expiration' and deducted a $16,600 standard deduction, a $3,200 aged addition and $10,600 in personal exemptions, totaling $30,400. That left $1,002.25 taxed at 10%. The TCJA did not expire: P.L. 119-21 made the $0 exemption and the higher standard deduction permanent. The 2026 joint standard deduction is $32,200, which exceeds the $31,402.25 AGI, so tax is $0.

It counted $11,588 of Social Security as taxable by using the 85% formula, even though combined income of $36,677 is below the $44,000 joint second threshold. Only the 50% tier applies, so taxable Social Security is $2,338.25 and AGI is $31,402.25, not $40,652. It then used a sunset-era $20,400 deduction built from a $12,700 base, although its stated components sum to only $16,070. The actual 2026 joint standard deduction under P.L. 119-21 is $32,200, which exceeds the correct AGI and gives $0 tax.

The model named the correct SSI-related aged pathway but asserted rather than computed the SSI income test: applying the $20 general exclusion, the $65 earned-income exclusion, and the one-half earned-income disregard gives countable income of about $15,205 from Social Security plus about $14,500 from wages, roughly $2,475 per month, far above the couple SSI federal benefit rate and above Virginia's ~80% FPL aged/blind/disabled limit, which is why SSI received is 0 and medicaid_category is NONE. It compounded this by treating Medicare Savings Program status (QMB/SLMB) and medically needy spend-down as Medicaid-eligibility categories, neither of which is a qualifying pathway here, and by never noticing that household income at 2.05x FPL exceeds even the 100% FPL QMB test.

The model invented a rule that PolicyEngine's aged category is age-only with no income test; the aged/disabled pathway is SSI-linked and requires passing both the SSI income and asset tests, which this household fails with $44,289 of combined wages and Social Security. Because SSI is 0, no category attaches and medicaid_category resolves to NONE despite the head being 71.

The model supplied no rule at all and defaulted age 71 to Medicaid eligibility. Age 71 removes the head from the MAGI expansion adult group (which ends at 64) and routes eligibility to the SSI-linked aged pathway, whose income and asset tests this household fails, so the correct derivation yields no qualifying category; the model's answer is consistent with an age-alone heuristic that skips every income test.

The model equated Medicare Savings Program status with Medicaid eligibility, concluding the head qualifies "as a Medicare savings program recipient"; MSP buy-in is not a PolicyEngine Medicaid eligibility category, and the head qualifies through none of the actual pathways. It also mischaracterized $44,289 of combined wages and Social Security as low income when that is 2.05x FPL, above both the MAGI thresholds and the 100% FPL QMB limit it implicitly relied on.
The model correctly computed Social Security tax of $1,801.968 and Medicare tax of $421.428 but failed to add them correctly. Their sum rounds to $2,223.39, not $4,412.33.

The model understated employee FICA by failing to apply the combined 7.65% Social Security and Medicare rate accurately to all $29,064 of wages. The two components are $1,801.97 and $421.43, totaling $2,223.39 rather than $2,090.

The model used the correct 7.65% FICA rate but rounded the resulting liability to $2,220 instead of calculating and reporting the required dollar amount. Applying 7.65% to $29,064 yields $2,223.396 before component-level cent rounding and $2,223.39 from the separately rounded Social Security and Medicare components.

The model incorrectly treated reaching full retirement age as an exemption from employee Social Security and Medicare taxes. Wages remain subject to FICA regardless of retirement age, producing $1,801.97 of Social Security tax and $421.43 of Medicare tax.

The model incorrectly bypassed the gross-income eligibility limit because both household members are elderly and proceeded directly to a speculative net-income calculation. It also treated the mortgage balance as though it established deductible shelter expenses, even though no rent, mortgage payment, property tax, insurance, or utility expense was listed; the $44,289 gross income instead fails the threshold and yields value = 0.

The model correctly computed that the $44,289 household MAGI exceeds 138% FPL for a couple, then overrode its own finding by asserting an aged pathway that tests the spouse's individual income ('spouse with no own income may qualify'). The SSI-related aged/blind/disabled test counts the couple's combined countable income under spousal deeming, not the spouse's zero personal earnings, and Virginia's ABD standard of roughly 80% FPL (about $17,300 for two) is failed by $44,289 by a factor of 2.5; with $0 SSI received, the SSI-recipient route is closed as well.

The model identified the correct pathway, Virginia's aged/blind/disabled category, but misstated its income limit, claiming $15,225 of Social Security plus $29,064 of wages sits 'well under the ABD income and resource limits for a couple after standard disregards.' Virginia's ABD categorically needy standard is about 80% FPL (roughly $17,300 annually for a couple), and the SSI disregards ($20 general, $65 plus half the remainder on earnings) still leave about $29,100 of countable annual income, so the couple fails the income test by more than $10,000; the resource check the model relied on is irrelevant once income disqualifies.

The model invented a rule, asserting that PolicyEngine places everyone 65+ in an 'aged eligibility category, which carries no income test.' No Medicaid category is conferred by age alone: the 65+ non-MAGI route requires SSI receipt or countable income within the state's SSI-related ABD standard (about 80% FPL) plus the $3,000 couple resource limit, and with $0 SSI and $44,289 of household income the engine assigns medicaid_category = NONE.

The model applied no eligibility test at all, defaulting a 69-year-old to 'potentially eligible' on age alone. Running the actual tests yields ineligibility on both branches: age 69 falls outside the 19-64 expansion adult group and the MAGI of 2.05x FPL exceeds the 138% FPL ceiling, while the non-MAGI aged route fails because SSI received is $0 and $44,289 of couple income is far above Virginia's roughly 80% FPL ABD standard.

The model conflated the Medicare Savings Programs with Medicaid eligibility, reasoning that the spouse 'qualifies for Medicaid as Medicare savings program recipient in Virginia.' MSP premium assistance is not a Medicaid eligibility category here, and the household fails it regardless: the QMB limit is 100% FPL while this couple sits at 2.05x FPL. The model also called the 69-year-old 'eligible for Medicare soon' when Medicare eligibility attached at 65, and it never applied any income test to the actual aged/blind/disabled pathway.

The model incorrectly treated 40 quarters of Medicare-covered employment as a prerequisite for Medicare eligibility rather than a condition for premium-free Part A. Under the requested PolicyEngine rule, the spouse's age of 69 satisfies the age-65 Medicare eligibility criterion, so the unlisted work history does not change the result.

Substituted "two $1,000 aged exemptions" for Virginia's $12,000-per-person age deduction under Va. Code § 58.1-322.02(10)-(11); the additional 65+ exemption is $800 and sits on top of that age deduction, which is unreduced here because AFYA of $29,064 is far below the $75,000 joint phase-out. Two full $12,000 age deductions exceed the $29,064 of Virginia AGI on their own, so taxable income is $0 rather than the $9,164 it computed. It also ran the 2% bracket to $5,000 when Virginia's 2% bracket stops at $3,000.

Carried federal AGI of $31,402.25 straight into Virginia without the § 58.1-322.02(4) subtraction for the $2,338.25 of federally taxable Social Security, so its Virginia AGI is $2,338 too high. It then allowed only $21,484 of total deductions — less than the $24,000 of age deductions alone, since both spouses are 65+ and AFYA of $29,064 sits below the $75,000 joint threshold. Correct Virginia AGI of $29,064 less $24,000 of age deductions plus the standard deduction and exemptions leaves $0 taxable income and $0 tax.

Gave no derivation, and its $560 corresponds to roughly $13,800 of Virginia taxable income ($60 + $60 + 5% of $8,800) — that is $29,064 of Virginia AGI reduced only by a standard deduction and personal exemptions, with no age deduction at all. Virginia's $12,000 age deduction applies to each spouse here because both are 65+ and AFYA of $29,064 is below the $75,000 joint reduction threshold, so $24,000 alone drives taxable income to $0.

Took the Virginia Social Security subtraction correctly but invented an offset in which the head's $12,000 age deduction is consumed by the $15,225 of Social Security benefits received; Virginia reduces the age deduction only for adjusted federal AGI over $75,000 on a joint return, and that measure excludes taxable Social Security entirely, so each spouse keeps the full $12,000. It also applied the $8,500 single standard deduction to a joint return. With $24,000 of age deductions against $29,064 of Virginia AGI, taxable income is $0, not $6,704.

Its $250.20 implies about $7,600 of Virginia taxable income, i.e. roughly $21,460 of total deductions against $29,064 of Virginia AGI — consistent with a single $12,000 age deduction plus the standard deduction and exemptions, not the "two age deductions" its explanation claims. Both spouses are 65 or older and combined AFYA of $29,064 is below the $75,000 joint phase-out, so $24,000 of age deductions applies and by itself exceeds Virginia AGI, leaving $0 of taxable income and $0 of tax.

Treated Virginia's age benefit as the $1,600 of "age/blind additions" — the two $800 additional 65+ exemptions — and never claimed the separate $12,000-per-person age deduction of § 58.1-322.02(10)-(11), which is unreduced because AFYA of $29,064 is far under the $75,000 joint threshold. Adding the missing $24,000 to its own $16,000 standard deduction and $1,860 of exemptions eliminates the $9,600 of taxable income it computed, so the tax is $0 rather than $350.

Put the entire $15,225 of Social Security into federal AGI for a $44,289 starting point when only $2,338.25 is federally taxable under the 50% tier, and then never applied Virginia's subtraction for that taxable portion — Virginia AGI is $29,064. It also discarded its own branch that used the correct $24,000 of age deductions and submitted $739.15, a figure none of its three calculations ($449.37, $33.78, and the $10,989 taxable-income branch) produces. Virginia AGI of $29,064 less $24,000 of age deductions plus the standard deduction and exemptions yields $0 taxable income and $0 tax.

It computed the return as a single filer — stating "only the head's income is relevant" — applying the single-filer $25,000/$34,000 provisional-income thresholds and a $20,550 single 65+ standard deduction instead of joint treatment, and it also carried the $24,000 disability benefits into both provisional income and includible income after asserting they were excluded. On the joint return with the disability and veterans benefits excluded, provisional income is $40,780, taxable Social Security is 50% × ($40,780 − $32,000) = $4,390, and AGI of $23,130 falls below the $35,500 MFJ standard deduction ($32,200 + two $1,650 age additions), before the $12,000 senior deduction, so tax is $0 rather than $4,427.

It treated the $24,000 disability benefits as taxable, which raised provisional income to $64,780, past the $44,000 MFJ threshold, and produced $23,663 of taxable Social Security instead of the $4,390 that the 50%-tier calculation yields at the true $40,780 provisional income. It then subtracted a pre-TCJA deduction stack — a $15,650 standard deduction plus two $5,050 personal exemptions, which have been repealed since 2018 — and applied a 15% bracket that no longer exists, when the actual 2026 MFJ deductions ($32,200 + $3,300 age additions + $12,000 senior deduction) exceed the $23,130 AGI and zero out the tax.

Its reasoning reached the correct conclusion — the 2026 married-both-65+ deduction exceeds AGI, so tax before refundable credits is $0 — and its explanation ends "value = 0," but the submitted numeric value was $120.30. The scored answer diverges from the model's own stated derivation, so this is a contract violation between explanation and submitted value rather than a substantive tax error.

It counted the $24,000 disability benefits as taxable, driving provisional income above the $44,000 MFJ threshold and forcing the 85%-tier Social Security inclusion of $23,663 rather than the 50%-tier $4,390 that $40,780 of provisional income produces. It then reduced the resulting $66,403 by $29,100 of "standard deduction, personal exemptions, and senior additions" — personal exemptions are repealed — and applied a nonexistent 15% bracket; with the disability and veterans benefits excluded, AGI of $23,130 is below the $35,500 MFJ standard deduction and the tax is $0.
